Here is the core signal path: Microphones pick up external sound and convert it to an electrical analog signal, which is then digitized into a discrete audio stream. This digital data is fed into a digital signal processor (DSP) that analyzes the waveform in real-time to identify the frequency and phase of the incoming noise. The DSP then generates an "anti-noise" signal that is the exact inverse of the detected noise (180 degrees out of phase). Finally, this anti-noise signal is sent through the speaker drivers, where it combines with the original external noise to create destructive interference, effectively canceling the sound out.

The primary trade-off is latency; if the system takes too long to process the incoming sound, the cancellation becomes ineffective because the noise has already passed. Additionally, there is a computational cost to the DSP, which can limit battery life and restrict the number of microphones that can be used simultaneously without significant processing delays.
